==English== {{wp|,+ (mechanics),+ (biology),+ (linguistics)}} ===Etymology=== {{etymon|en|:inh|enm:destresse>>>|tree=1}} From a shortening of {{inh|en|enm|destresse}}, borrowed from {{der|en|fro|destrecier}}, from {{der|en|la|distringō||to stretch out}}.Keil, R.M.K. (2004) [http://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/bsc/jan/2004/00000045/00000006/art00013 Coping and stress: a conceptual analysis] Journal of Advanced Nursing, 45(6), 659–665 This form probably coalesced with {{inh|en|enm|stresse}}, from {{der|en|fro|estrece||narrowness}}, from {{der|en|la-vul|*strictia}}, from {{der|en|la|strictus||narrow}}. Displaced native {{noncog|ang|swēġ||accent, stress}}, though strictly in the [[grammatical]] sense. In the sense of "mental strain" or “disruption”, used occasionally in the 1920s and 1930s by psychologists, including {{w|Walter Cannon}} (1934); in “biological threat”, used by endocrinologist {{w|Hans Selye}}, by metaphor with stress in physics (force on an object) in the 1930s, and popularized by same in the 1950s. ===Pronunciation=== * {{IPA|en|/ˈstɹɛs/|/ˈʃt͡ʃɹɛs/|a=UK}} * {{audio|en|LL-Q1860 (eng)-Xavier hillier-stress.wav|a=UK}} * {{IPA|en|/stɹɛs/|a=GA}} * {{audio|en|en-us-stress.ogg|a=US}} * {{rhymes|en|ɛs|s=1}} ===Noun=== {{en-noun|~}} # {{lb|en|biology}} A physical, chemical, infective agent aggressing an organism. # {{lb|en|biology}} Aggression toward an organism resulting in a response in an attempt to restore previous conditions. # {{senseid|en|Q206175}} {{lb|en|countable|physics}} The internal distribution of force across a small boundary per unit area of that boundary ([[pressure]]) within a body. It causes [[strain]] or [[deformation]] and is typically symbolised by [[σ]] or [[τ]]. #: {{hypo|en|tensile stress|mul:σ|shear stress|mul:τ}} #: {{cot|en|strain|deformation|force|pressure}} # {{lb|en|countable|physics}} Force externally applied to a body which cause internal stress within the body. # {{lb|en|uncountable}} Emotional pressure suffered by a human being or other animal. #: {{ux|en|Go easy on him, he's been under a lot of '''stress''' lately.}} #* {{quote-journal|en|doi=10.1007/s12144-024-07110-1|title=Which types of family caregivers are more prone to developing depression? Leveraging non-financial social support to mitigate depression|work=Current Psychology|date=2024-12-16|author=Amanda M. Y. Chu; Damen H. Y. Woo; Agnes Tiwari; Helina Yuk; Mike K. P. So|passage=Lazarus and Folkman’s transactional model of '''stress''' and coping describes psychological '''stress''' as “a particular relationship between the person and the environment that is appraised as taxing or exceeding his or her resources and endangering his or her well-being” (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984, p.19). According to these authors, the essence of inducing '''stress''' is how a person appraises the situation and whether he or she has the physical and mental ability to cope with the problem.}} # {{senseid|en|broadest phonological sense}} {{lb|en|countable|phonetics|loosely}} A [[suprasegmental]] [[feature]] of a [[language]] having additional attention [[raise]]d to a [[sound]], [[word]] or word group [[by means of]] of [[loudness]], [[duration]] or [[pitch]]; [[phonological]] [[prominence]]. #: {{syn|en|emphasis|accent}} #: {{coi|en|lexical '''stress'''}};   {{coi|en|phrase '''stress''', prosodic '''stress'''}} #: {{ux|en|Some people put the '''stress''' on the first syllable of “controversy”; others put it on the second.}} # {{senseid|en|phonological sense that excludes pitch}} {{lb|en|countable|phonetics|strictly}} The [[suprasegmental]] [[feature]] of a [[language]] having additional attention [[raise]]d to a [[sound]] [[by means of]] [[loudness]] and/or [[duration]]; [[phonological]] [[prominence]] [[phonetically]] [[achieved]] by means of {{w|Dynamics (music)|dynamics}} as distinct from {{w|Pitch (music)|pitch}}. #: {{syn|en|stress accent}} #: {{ant|en|pitch|pitch accent}} #* {{quote-book|en|date=09-07-2020|title=Historical Linguistics 2017: Selected Papers from the 23rd International Conference on Historical Linguistics, San Antonio, Texas, 31 July – 4 August 2017|chapter=Parallel syncretism in early Indo-European|author=Steve Rapaport|editor=Bridget Drinka|page=59|pageurl=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Historical_Linguistics_2017/3onrDwAAQBAJ?gbpv=1&pg=PA59|doi=10.1075/cilt.350.03rap|passage=The shift from pitch to '''stress''' appears to happen before the other obliques begin merging in the Proto-Italic, Proto-Germanic, Primitive Irish, and Middle Indo-Aryan. But further investigation into the timeline of sound changes […] shows that, at least in Germanic, the oblique and core noun stems sound quite unpredictably different in all these families by the time of the crucial accent shift from pitch to '''stress'''. […] once a language becomes '''stress'''-sensitive, there seems to be a strong tendency in early Indo-European languages to shift the '''stress''' to the first syllable. This change happens shortly after the change to '''stress''' accent in Proto-Germanic, Proto-Italic, and Proto-Celtic, and even Thessalian, with evidence from Dybo's Law and Verner's Law left behind to show that sound changes happened after the changes to '''stress''' accent.}} # {{lb|en|uncountable}} Emphasis placed on a particular point in an argument or discussion (whether spoken or written). # {{obsolete form of|en|distress}}. #* {{RQ:Spenser Faerie Queene|3|2|passage=With this sad Hersal of his heavy '''stress''',
The warlike Damzel was empassion's sore,
And said; Sir Knight, your Cause is nothing less
Than is your Sorrow , certes if not more}} # {{lb|en|Scots law}} [[distress]]; the act of [[distrain]]ing; also, the thing distrained. ====Synonyms==== * {{sense|phonetics}} {{l|en|accent}},
